base: The Baseline Madness Index measures each team’s underlying strength using possession-level performance across the full season.
Eight core possession battles shape the profile: shooting efficiency, rebounding, ball security, and foul pressure on both ends of the floor.
The résumé then calibrates how much trust to place in that profile, anchoring extreme signals toward the tournament field when results are less proven.
matchup: The matchup-adjusted rating shows how those baseline profiles change when the two teams are evaluated against each other directly.
Five stylistic pressure channels — turnovers, rebounding, fouls, rim access, and perimeter variance — measure where one team can stress the other.
These pressures reshape the baseline comparison, revealing which team’s style gains leverage in this specific game environment.

glossary.title: Stat & Rule Glossary
glossary.help: Definitions for all metrics, rules, and analytical concepts used in the Madness Index.

entries.definition: A composite rating that summarizes a team’s tournament identity using baseline strength and profile breadth. MI is designed to be stable, comparable across teams, and readable as a single-number anchor.
A running record of evaluated matchups, capturing the teams, round context, and the system’s outputs at the time of analysis. It functions as an audit trail for recent comparisons.
An alternate evaluation state that allows manual adjustments without treating the result as an official matchup outcome. It is used for testing inputs, edge cases, and “what-if” scenarios.

A team’s baseline matchup starting point before opponent-specific interaction effects are added. In the current engine, it begins with foundation, which is the team’s adjusted MI Efficiency Margin, then applies Résumé Base Trust to calibrate that raw baseline toward the field mean. So it is not just 'how good the team is', but 'how strong the team’s normalized internal profile is after structural adjustment and résumé calibration'.

A team’s final matchup score after adding opponent-specific interaction adjustments to Baseline MI. The interaction adjustment is also scaled by résumé-based interaction trust, so Matchup MI is the model’s final score for this exact pairing, not a general team power rating.

The gap between the two teams’ final Matchup MI scores. In the engine, this is the final margin after both baseline and interaction adjustments have been applied. It is the model’s final separation signal for the matchup.

A field-normalized offensive rebounding driver in MI Offensive Efficiency. It measures how much a team creates second-chance value relative to the field, and it carries a 0.35 weight inside the offensive efficiency base.
A field-normalized shot-efficiency driver in MI Offensive Efficiency. It reflects shooting efficiency relative to the field and carries a 0.30 weight inside the offensive efficiency base.
Not raw turnover rate by itself, but the inverted, field-normalized turnover signal used offensively so that lower turnover rate becomes better. It carries a 0.25 weight in MI Offensive Efficiency.
A field-normalized foul-pressure / line-access driver in MI Offensive Efficiency. It is the offensive ability to generate free-throw opportunities relative to the field, weighted 0.10.

A structural balance adjustment built from the spread of the team’s four offensive driver z-scores: offensive rebounding, eFG, turnover avoidance, and free-throw rate. Lower dispersion means a more balanced offensive profile and earns a stronger offensive breadth bonus; higher dispersion reduces it. This bonus is then added directly to MI Offensive Efficiency.
The opponent shooting efficiency a team allows, adjusted for the added value of three-point shots. Def eFG% reflects how well a defense limits quality shot conversion.
A field-normalized defensive rebounding driver in MI Defensive Efficiency. It reflects how well a team ends possessions.

A field-normalized defensive pressure driver built from opponent turnover creation proxy data. In the core traits layer, it is the defensive turnover-generation component inside MI Defensive Efficiency.

An orientation-adjusted defensive discipline driver. It is based on opponent free-throw rate allowed, inverted so that allowing fewer free throws is better. It carries a 0.10 weight inside MI Defensive Efficiency.

A structural balance adjustment built from the spread of the team’s four defensive driver z-scores: opponent eFG suppression, defensive rebounding, turnover creation, and free-throw prevention. Lower dispersion means the defense is more evenly supported across battlefields, so the defensive breadth bonus is stronger. That bonus is then added directly to MI Defensive Efficiency.

A separate matchup-environment score from 1–100 created by equally weighting four normalized volatility drivers: tempo, 3-point environment, EPR environment, and extra scoring chances. It does not directly decide the winner; it describes how unstable or swing-prone the matchup environment is.

A volatility driver built from both the average field-relative tempo level in the matchup and the tempo gap between the two teams. So it measures not just pace, but how much pace itself may destabilize the game environment.

A volatility driver built from average 3-point rate, average share of points from 3, the gap in 3-point rate between teams, and a small 3P% modifier that only matters when the matchup is already high-volume from deep. So it is really a 3-point environment / reliance signal, not just simple dependence.

A volatility driver built from the matchup’s average field-relative EPR and the gap between the teams’ EPR values. The engine inverts the average component, so weaker possession efficiency environments increase volatility.
A volatility driver built from average and gap values in extra scoring chances per game. Higher second-chance / extra-possession environments raise volatility.
A static identity score that measures how strongly a team’s profile supports a Cinderella-style upset narrative. CIS reflects underdog viability as an identity signal, not a prediction.
A static identity score that measures how strongly a team’s profile supports favorite-level stability and control. FAS reflects chalk reliability as an identity signal, not a prediction.
A round-aware identity score that updates Cinderella alignment based on opponent, path, and current round framing. LCI reflects the Cinderella signal in the present matchup context.
A round-aware identity score that updates favorite alignment based on opponent, path, and current round framing. LFI reflects the favorite signal in the present matchup context.

The identity label applied when a matchup does not cleanly resolve into standard Cinderella-versus-favorite framing. It indicates a non-standard identity state such as mirror, neutral, or chaos conditions.

A field-normalized résumé quality signal built from stabilized Q1/Q2 performance, weighted quality-win volume, bad-loss resistance, opponent-quality share, win percentage, and schedule hardness. In the current engine, résumé context does not directly replace baseline performance; instead it produces trust factors that calibrate baseline, interactions, and confidence.
The résumé classification band assigned to a team based on its résumé context strength. Tiers provide a compact summary of résumé quality without describing specific results.
A set of named flags that tag notable profile patterns that can matter in tournament play. Marks are descriptive signals, not standalone ratings or guarantees.
A profile mark indicating a team’s offense is built around a narrow scoring shape or limited scoring pathways. It describes an offense that can be easier to map if its primary option is contained.
A profile mark indicating perimeter outcomes are highly variable or structurally vulnerable within the profile. It flags a team whose outside layer is less reliable or more matchup-sensitive.
A profile mark indicating low or inconsistent three-point shot conversion relative to peer baselines. It describes a profile that does not reliably generate scoring from the arc.
A profile mark indicating a defense that concedes avoidable advantages through fouls, breakdowns, or poor containment. It flags defensive execution risk rather than scheme identity.
A profile mark indicating the interior defense yields efficiency or access near the rim relative to baseline expectations. It describes a profile that can struggle to consistently protect the paint.
A profile mark indicating the defense allows elevated perimeter shot quality or volume compared to baseline. It flags an outside-containment vulnerability rather than shooting variance.
A profile mark indicating performance is less stable when pace rises or possession flow becomes chaotic. It flags a profile that can lose efficiency under speed or disruption.

These are directional, opponent-specific channels. They do not just ask, “Is Team A good at X?” They ask, “How much does Team A’s strength in X pressure Team B’s vulnerability in X, and how much does the reverse apply?” They are also gated by baseline difference, so interactions matter less in lopsided matchups.

An interaction channel that compares one team’s 3-point volume / scoring reliance against the opponent’s ability to limit opponent 3-point rate and accuracy. It is not merely “who shoots more threes,” but whether one side can impose a high-variance perimeter environment on the other.

An interaction channel that compares one team’s interior access profile, which is driven by non-blocked 2-point creation, 2-point scoring share, and eFG support, against the opponent’s rim protection and interior shot suppression.

An interaction channel that combines one team’s turnover-forcing ability with the opponent’s turnover vulnerability. In the engine, pressure side includes forced-turnover proxies and steal pressure, while vulnerability side includes the opponent’s turnover rate and assist/possession shape.

An interaction channel that compares one team’s offensive rebounding pressure against the opponent’s defensive rebounding resistance. It models extra-possession stress at the glass, not general rebounding quality in isolation.

An interaction channel that compares one team’s free-throw drawing profile against the opponent’s foul-discipline vulnerability. In the engine it blends free-throw rate and FT scoring share on the offensive side against opponent FT-rate prevention on the defensive side.

formula.card: Each Madness Index score starts from MI_base, a blend of Core Traits, Breadth, and Résumé Context. Matchup-specific interaction leverage is added on top to get MI_matchup.

core.card: Core Traits measure who a team is possession-to-possession: offensive efficiency, defensive efficiency, shooting quality, and possession control.
core.tile: This tile shows each core stat, how it grades versus the 64-team field, and how much weight it carries in the Core composite.

breadth.card: Breadth rewards teams that are strong in multiple core areas at once rather than leaning on a single spike. More overlapping strengths create a larger Breadth bonus.
breadth.tile: The Breadth summary highlights how many core metrics clear the above-average threshold and how much bonus that coverage adds.

resume.card: Résumé Context Score V2 evaluates how a team’s results hold up under competitive context. It blends stabilized Q1 and Q2 performance, quality-win volume, bad-loss resistance, opponent-quality share, win percentage, and strength of schedule into a single field-relative résumé index.
resume.tile: This tile summarizes how the team’s résumé reads against the tournament field once quality wins, bad-loss resistance, opponent mix, win percentage, and schedule strength are standardized together. That résumé index then determines the team’s résumé trust tier.

Elite: This résumé combines high-end win quality, meaningful quality-win volume, and strong resistance to damaging losses. It reflects a profile that remains highly credible once schedule hardness and opponent mix are fully accounted for.
Strong: This résumé shows durable quality through strong upper-quadrant performance and solid contextual support. It reflects a profile whose results continue to hold up well after schedule strength and résumé depth are standardized.
Above Average: This résumé carries legitimate strength through a healthy mix of quality wins and stable contextual support. It reflects a profile that is supported more often than challenged once the full résumé environment is weighed.
Average: This résumé lands near the middle of the field once quality, volume, schedule, and loss resistance are blended together. It reflects a profile with neither especially strong validation nor especially strong résumé fragility.
Weak: This résumé shows limited contextual strength once upper-end results, bad-loss resistance, and schedule quality are evaluated together. It reflects a profile that does not gain much trust from its full résumé composition relative to the field.
Fragile: This résumé struggles to establish strong contextual credibility once quality-win signals and damaging-loss pressure are fully incorporated. It reflects a profile whose résumé support weakens meaningfully when compared against the full tournament field.
fallback: This résumé tier reflects how the team’s full Résumé Context Score compares with the rest of the tournament field.

marks.card: Profile Marks are diagnostic flags. They do not change the score directly, but they reveal structural strengths or vulnerabilities that may matter in specific matchups.
marks.tile: Each badge reflects a repeatable pattern in the stats (for example, rim softness, turnover fragility, or cold perimeter shooting). Use them as quick scouting shortcuts.

identity.tile: Tournament Identity blends CIS (Cinderella Index Score) and FAS (Favorite Alignment Score) into a single snapshot of how this team tends to show up in a bracket.
